practice.context: A story opens, “At midnight the lighthouse blinked twice, although no keeper had lived there for years.” Which feature most clearly supports an imaginative purpose?
practice.correct: A mysterious invented event that creates curiosity about what may happen next.
distractors: A numbered list of verified lighthouse statistics.
A labelled diagram explaining lens parts.
A call to sign a petition about coastal lighting.
practice.rationale: Imaginative texts often build characters, settings and events to engage readers in an invented world.
practice.hint: Ask what feature helps the text tell or develop an imagined experience.

practice.context: An information page about frogs uses the headings “Habitat”, “Diet” and “Life cycle”. Why are these headings useful?
practice.correct: They group related facts so readers can locate information efficiently.
distractors: They make the page fictional.
They prove every fact is equally important.
They persuade readers to buy a frog.
practice.rationale: Headings organise an informative text and help readers navigate to a needed section.
practice.hint: Notice how navigation features help a reader find or organise information.

practice.context: A fact sheet shows a labelled cross-section of a volcano beside a paragraph about magma and vents. What is the image doing?
practice.correct: It adds spatial information that helps readers connect the named parts to their positions.
distractors: It replaces the need for any written explanation.
It turns the fact sheet into a narrative.
It proves the volcano will erupt soon.
practice.rationale: Informative visuals can complement words by showing relationships that are easier to understand spatially.
practice.hint: Compare what the visual adds to what the words already tell you.

practice.context: A poster says, “Choose refillable bottles: one small change can reduce plastic waste,” beside a bold heading and an image of reusable bottles. Which feature most supports its persuasive purpose?
practice.correct: A direct call to action linked to a reason.
distractors: A setting description that builds suspense.
A neutral glossary of bottle materials only.
A chronological recount of yesterday’s lunch.
practice.rationale: Persuasive texts often make a position clear and support a requested action with reasons or evidence.
practice.hint: Look for language that asks the audience to think or act in a particular way.

practice.context: A recipe has an ingredient list followed by numbered steps. Which explanation best connects structure to purpose?
practice.correct: The list shows what is needed and the numbered steps show the order for carrying out the procedure.
distractors: The structure creates imaginary characters.
The numbers are decorative and do not affect use.
The list is mainly designed to express an opinion.
practice.rationale: Characteristic text structures are chosen because they help a text achieve its purpose.
practice.hint: Ask why this structure makes the text easier to use for its intended purpose.

practice.context: A museum webpage includes a short paragraph, a historical photograph with a caption and a timeline. Which statement best explains the combined features?
practice.correct: The paragraph explains, the caption identifies the photograph, and the timeline places events in sequence.
distractors: All three features repeat exactly the same information.
The photograph alone proves every claim on the page.
The timeline makes the page imaginative rather than informative.
practice.rationale: Multimodal informative texts combine features that contribute different but connected kinds of information.
practice.hint: Identify what each mode contributes and how the parts work together.

test.context: A short story uses dialogue, a problem and a surprising resolution. Which statement best explains why these are characteristic imaginative features?
test.correct: They develop characters and events so readers can follow an invented experience.
distractors: They organise facts into categories.
They provide directions in exact order.
They present a claim with supporting statistics.
test.rationale: Dialogue, problems and resolutions are common ways imaginative texts develop story meaning.
test.hint: Match the feature to the purpose it helps the text achieve.

test.context: An online article has a contents menu, subheadings and hyperlinks to definitions. What is their main purpose?
test.correct: To help readers navigate sections and access supporting information.
distractors: To make all readers follow one fixed path.
To create suspense about a fictional ending.
To replace the need for clear paragraphs.
test.rationale: Navigation features help readers locate, move between and clarify information.
test.hint: Think about what the reader can do more efficiently because of the feature.

test.context: A weather report places a map with colour bands beside a written forecast. Why can the map be useful?
test.correct: It shows where different conditions are expected, adding location information to the written forecast.
distractors: It proves the forecast cannot change.
It is only decorative because words already exist.
It changes the report into a persuasive advertisement.
test.rationale: A visual can add location, comparison or pattern information that complements written explanation.
test.hint: Ask what information is easier to see in the visual than in prose.

test.context: A campaign text says, “Support the school garden because it gives students a place to learn outdoors,” followed by three evidence points. Which feature most clearly serves the persuasive purpose?
test.correct: A position supported by reasons and evidence.
distractors: An unresolved mystery.
A list of character traits.
A sequence of fictional events.
test.rationale: Persuasive texts state a position and support it with reasons or evidence designed for an audience.
test.hint: Look for the claim and the support offered for it.
